passage: By the time Esther's aunt came out to the courtyard with the washing basket, the skipping rope lay in the dust and both children were talking at once. "She grabbed it when it was my go!" "He was holding it for ages, he always keeps it!" "You never let anyone finish a turn!" "You always cry when you lose!" Abebe's voice climbed higher with every sentence. Esther didn't even look at him; she was counting on her fingers all the times he had cheated at games last month. The aunt set down the basket. "Wait. What happened first?" Neither answered the question. Each was already opening their mouth to add one more thing the other had done.

qa.q: What were the children arguing over in the courtyard?
qa.a: They were arguing over the skipping rope, which lay in the dust.

qa.q: How was Esther feeling as she counted on her fingers instead of looking at Abebe?
qa.a: She was resentful and set on winning, collecting all the times she thought he had cheated last month instead of listening to him.

qa.q: What could the aunt try so the argument does not climb any higher?
qa.a: She could ask each child to tell their side one at a time while the other only listens, and repeat back what she heard before anyone replies.

qa.q: What is it like for Abebe when Esther won't even look at him?
qa.a: Abebe probably feels unheard, which may be why his voice keeps climbing; he is shouting to be noticed as much as to win.

grounding: Shows two children each telling the story so only the other is to blame, trading 'always' and 'never' while nobody listens.

passage: In the corridor outside the Class 5 staff room, Wasim and Devika stood by the water cooler, both red in the face. The cricket bat between them had a crack along the handle. "Devika threw it on the ground after her turn, Ma'am, I saw!" "No, Wasim hit the wall with it! You always blame me for everything." "And you never admit anything!" Mrs Kulkarni, the games teacher, opened her mouth, but Wasim was already talking again, listing every broken thing from last term. Devika wasn't listening; her lips were moving as she got her next answer ready. Neither of them looked at the bat anymore. It had become a contest over who would get the last word.

qa.q: What was wrong with the cricket bat?
qa.a: The cricket bat had a crack along the handle.

qa.q: How was Devika feeling as her lips moved?
qa.a: She felt defensive and set on winning, red in the face and getting her next answer ready instead of listening to Wasim.

qa.q: How could Mrs Kulkarni turn this moment around?
qa.a: She could set the bat aside, ask both children to drink some water, and give each a turn to speak without interruption before deciding anything.

qa.q: If you were Mrs Kulkarni, what would you notice about the argument?
qa.a: The teacher would notice that neither child looks at the bat anymore; the fight is now only about getting the last word.

grounding: Shows two children in a school corridor each blaming the other with 'always' and 'never', too busy preparing defences to listen.

passage:
The lunch supervisor at the London primary school crouched between them by the wall. "One at a time. Emeka?"
"Rosa kicked the ball over the fence on purpose, and now we can't play, and she always does that."
"I did NOT. You passed it badly! You never pass properly, then you blame me!"
"You always say that!"
"Because it's always true!"
The supervisor tried again. "Rosa, what happened just before?"
But Emeka was already talking over her, remembering a game from last week, and Rosa was shaking her head, lips moving, getting her next line ready. Neither of them was looking at the other.

qa.q: Who crouched between Emeka and Rosa?
qa.a: The lunch supervisor at the London primary school.

qa.q: What does Emeka's talking over Rosa suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels defensive and angry, desperate to be seen as the one in the right, so he is busy preparing his case rather than listening.

qa.q: What turning point could the supervisor offer at this stage?
qa.a: The supervisor could stop the storytelling for a moment and ask each child to take a breath or say what the other one said, so they have to listen before defending.

qa.q: What is Rosa experiencing as Emeka keeps talking?
qa.a: She feels unfairly blamed and unheard, which makes her dig in and get her own defence ready.

grounding: Two children each tell the story so the other is to blame, using always and never, and neither listens because both are busy defending.

passage:
In the changing room of the dance academy, the teacher had stepped out for one minute.
"You stood on my foot in the spin, Alka, that's why I fell."
"Shreya, you came in late on the count! You never listen to the count!"
"And you always stand too close!"
Their voices bounced off the lockers. A younger girl pulled her bag closer and slipped out.
"It's your fault Ma'am shouted at the whole row."
"No, it's yours."
Shreya's cheeks were hot. She was not really hearing Alka anymore; she was lining up everything Alka had done wrong since the first class, ready to fire back.

qa.q: Where were Shreya and Alka arguing?
qa.a: In the changing room of the dance academy.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling as the argument went on?
qa.a: She felt hot-faced and angry, and defensive enough that she stopped hearing Alka and started listing all of Alka's past mistakes.

qa.q: What could help at this stage, before it gets worse?
qa.a: One of them could stop and ask, "What did you see in the spin?" or they could wait for the teacher, so that someone listens instead of just blaming.

qa.q: What is Alka likely experiencing right now?
qa.a: She probably feels blamed for the fall and embarrassed about the teacher's shouting, so she pushes the fault back onto Shreya.

grounding: After a fall in dance class, two girls each tell the story so only the other is at fault, with rising voices and no listening.

passage:
Monday: Nirmala and Kalyani shared one cycle to school, taking turns to pedal. Kalyani's dupatta caught in the chain near the bridge and they both fell in the dust.
Wednesday: At Nani's house, both told the story again. "She was going too fast," said Kalyani. "She never holds the seat properly!" said Nirmala. "You always tie your dupatta loose!" "You always ride like a goat!" Nani tried to ask a question, and neither heard it.
Friday: They walked to school on separate sides of the road. Nirmala kept practising in her head what she would say if Kalyani started again.

qa.q: What caught in the cycle chain on Monday?
qa.a: Kalyani's dupatta caught in the chain near the bridge.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling on Friday as she walked to school?
qa.a: She still felt hurt and defensive, rehearsing her side in her head in case Kalyani started again.

qa.q: What turning point could Nani offer on Wednesday?
qa.a: Nani could ask them both to stop and each say how the fall felt, not whose fault it was, before either says "always" again.

qa.q: What might Kalyani be experiencing by Friday?
qa.a: She is probably also sore and lonely on the other side of the road, holding on to her version because letting go feels like losing.

grounding: Over a week, two girls turn a small cycle fall into a blame contest full of always and never, and both keep rehearsing defences instead of listening.

passage:
Anirban, come here, your Madhuri Dadi will tell you something about fighting with your sister.

When I was ten, my brother Nitin and I broke Ma's glass lamp. We were chasing each other round the courtyard. Ma came running, and at once I said, "He pushed me into it!"

Nitin shouted, "She started it! She always starts it!"

"You never let me play! You always cheat!"

We got louder and louder. Ma was standing right there, but neither of us looked at her. I was busy thinking up the next thing to say. So was Nitin. Neither of us heard a single word the other said.

Finally Ma sat down on the step and said nothing at all. That silence stopped us. Then she asked, "Who wants to sweep the glass?" We both did it together.

qa.q: What did Madhuri and Nitin break?
qa.a: They broke Ma's glass lamp.

qa.q: What was Madhuri thinking about during the shouting?
qa.a: She was busy thinking up the next thing to say to defend herself, feeling defensive and angry rather than listening.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ma sitting down in silence; with no one to argue at, the children stopped, and sweeping together turned blame into a shared job.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt while they were shouting?
qa.a: Nitin probably felt angry and blamed, just as busy defending himself and just as unheard.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood quarrel where each child told the story so only the other was at fault, with 'always' and 'never' and no listening.
